read.sections.2.text.back: Every exchange depends on trust. The buyer trusts that the food is fresh and the scales are fair. The seller trusts that the payment is real. People also trust each other that promises will be kept, like Nadia's promise to help with learning to read. If people cheat, other people stop trusting them, and trade becomes harder for everyone. This is one reason many markets have rules about fair scales and measures. For thousands of years, markets have brought people together to trade. If people trade fairly, they can meet more needs, and communities become more connected.

People also trust each other to keep promises, like Nadia's promise to help with reading. If people cheat, others stop trusting them, and trade becomes harder for everyone. This is one reason many markets have rules about fair weights and measures. For thousands of years, markets have brought people together to trade. When people trade fairly, they meet more of their needs, and communities become more connected.

read.sections.0.text.back: No person can make everything they use. Try thinking about a simple exercise book. One person makes the paper, another person brings the books to the market, and yet another person sells it. The things people exchange are goods and services. Goods are objects you can touch and use, like rice or a pencil. A service is something useful that someone does for another person, like teaching, fixing a bicycle, or cutting hair. A producer is a person or group who makes goods or provides services. A consumer is a person who uses or buys them. At Lakeside Market, Ana is a producer when she sells tomatoes. She is also a consumer when she buys rice.
read.sections.0.text.source: No person can make everything they use. Think about a simple notebook. One person made the paper, another carried the notebooks to a market and another sold them. The things people exchange are goods and services. A good is a thing you can touch and use, such as rice or a pencil. A service is something useful that a person does for someone else, such as teaching, fixing a bicycle or cutting hair. A producer is a person or group that makes a good or provides a service. A consumer is a person who uses or buys it. At Lakeside Market, Ana is a producer when she sells tomatoes. She is also a consumer when she buys rice.

Ana grows tomatoes, so she is a producer. When she buys rice, she is a consumer.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: No one can make everything they use. Think of a notebook. Many people help to make it and sell it. People swap goods and services. A good is a thing you can touch, like rice. A service is work a person does for you, like teaching. A producer makes a good or does a service. A consumer uses or buys it. Ana grows tomatoes, so she is a producer. When she buys rice, she is a consumer.

read.sections.1.text.back: Sometimes people exchange goods or services without using money. This is called barter. At Lakeside Market, Kofi swaps some of his bread for some of Sara's eggs. Ravi fixes Nadia's bicycle, and in return Nadia helps Ravi's younger sibling learn to read. Barter still happens in many places today. However, barter has a problem: both sides must each want what the other side has, at the same time. Leo has fish and wants rice, but the rice seller does not want fish. Money solves this problem. Leo can sell his fish, then use the money to buy rice. Money also helps people compare prices and store value for later.
read.sections.1.text.source: Sometimes people swap goods or services without using money. This is called barter. At Lakeside Market, Kofi swaps some of his bread for some of Sara's eggs. Ravi fixes Nadia's bicycle, and in return Nadia helps Ravi's sister with reading. Barter still happens in many places today. However, it has a problem: both people must want what the other person has, at the same time. Leo has fish and wants rice, but the rice seller does not want fish. Money solves this problem. Leo can sell his fish and use the money to buy rice. Money also helps people compare prices and keep value for later.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Sometimes people swap goods without money. This is called barter. Kofi gives Sara bread, and Sara gives him eggs. Ravi fixes a bicycle, and Nadia helps his younger sibling read. But barter has a problem. Both people must want the other's thing. Leo has fish. He wants rice. The rice seller does not want fish. Here money helps. Leo can sell his fish to get money. Then he can buy rice.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Sometimes people swap things with no money. This is called barter. Kofi gives Sara bread, and she gives him eggs. Ravi fixes a bike, and Nadia helps his sister read. But barter has a problem. Both people must want what the other has. Leo has fish. He wants rice. The rice seller does not want fish. Money helps here. Leo can sell his fish for money. Then he can buy rice.

If someone cheats, people stop trusting them. Then trade becomes harder for everyone. Since very long ago, markets have brought many people together. If people trade fairly, they get more of what they need.

write.example.back: In this exchange, Ravi gives a service to Nadia. He fixes Nadia's bicycle. In return, Ravi's younger sister gets help learning to read from Nadia for one week. This exchange is barter because they exchange skills and do not use money. Trust helps because Ravi fixes the bicycle first. He trusts Nadia will keep her promise later. Without trust, Ravi might not want to help at all, and both of them would lose something useful.

watch.summary.back: This short video for younger learners explains goods and services. First, the video reminds you about needs and wants. Needs are things you must have to live, like food, water, and shelter. Wants are things you would like to have, like toys and games. People use money to get goods and services. Goods are objects people make or grow to sell, like food, books, and toys. Services are work people do for other people. Doctors help people stay healthy. Pilots fly planes. Cooks cook food. Then the video gives some puzzles. A book is a good, but a librarian gives a service when they help you find a book. Pizza is a good, but delivering it to your house is a service.
watch.summary.source: This short video for younger learners explains goods and services. First, it reminds you about needs and wants. Needs are things you must have to live, like food, water and a place to live. Wants are things you would like, like toys and games. People use money to get goods and services. Goods are things people make or grow to sell, like food, books and toys. Services are work people do for others. A doctor helps people stay healthy. A pilot flies a plane. A chef cooks food. Then the video gives some puzzles. A book is a good, but a librarian gives a service when they help you find one. A pizza is a good, but bringing it to your home is a service.

educatorNotes.1.source: The lesson does not say that barter always came before money. Many historians and anthropologists question the idea that whole communities once lived only by barter; gifts and credit were also common. Barter is shown as one way to exchange that still happens today.
educatorNotes.1.note: 'Gifts and credit' as 'pemberian dan utang'; 'kredit' is the other option. Please confirm. | Reviewer: 'pemberian dan utang' for 'gifts and credit': acceptable, but check 'utang' reads as normal lending between people, not as something negative.
educatorNotes.1.back: This lesson doesn't say that barter always existed before money. Many historians and anthropologists doubt the idea that there were once communities that lived entirely on barter alone; gifts and debt were also common. Barter is shown as one way of exchanging that still happens today.
